s: Tobit, a Naphtali man of the line of Tobiel, introduces himself as one carried captive from Thisbe to Nineveh in the days of Enemessar. He recounts that while his tribe turned to sacrificing to Baal, he alone went to Jerusalem for the feasts and gave his tithes and first fruits, and he later married Anna and fathered Tobias. In captivity he refused the Gentiles' bread, gained favor with Enemessar and served as his purchasing agent, and left ten talents of silver with Gabael in Rages of Media. Under Sennacherib he gave to the needy and secretly buried slain Israelites until a Ninevite informed on him, forcing him to flee and costing him all his goods except his wife Anna and son Tobias. After Sennacherib was killed by two of his sons, Sarchedonus reigned and appointed Tobit's kinsman Achiacharus over the kingdom's accounts, and Achiacharus secured Tobit's return to Nineveh.

Tobit, of the tribe of Naphtali, was carried captive to Nineveh, yet walked in truth and righteousness, going alone to Jerusalem for the feasts and giving tithes while his tribe sacrificed to Baal. He married Anna, fathered Tobias, refused the Gentiles' bread, and became Enemessar's purchasing agent. After burying the dead under Sennacherib he was informed on, fled, and lost all his goods save his wife and son, until Achiacharus enabled his return to Nineveh.

Enemessar was king of the Assyrians when Tobit was carried captive. The Most High gave Tobit favor in his sight, and Tobit served as his purchasing agent; after Enemessar died, his son Sennacherib reigned.

Nineveh is the Assyrian city to which Tobit, his kindred and his nation were carried captive. Dead Israelites were thrown out on its wall and Tobit buried them there, and it is where Achiacharus later called Tobit back.

Jerusalem is the house chosen out of all the tribes of Israel for sacrifice, with the temple of the Most High hallowed there for all ages. Tobit alone of his tribe went there often to the feasts, giving first fruits and tithes to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and to the sons of Levi, and spending a second tenth there each year.

Sennacherib succeeded his father Enemessar, and in his time the highways were troubled so Tobit could no longer go into Media. He killed many who fled from Judea and sought their bodies, and he sought Tobit to put him to death. Fifty-five days later two of his sons killed him and fled to the mountains of Ararat, and Sarchedonus his son reigned.

Achiacharus was Tobit's brother Anael's son, appointed by Sarchedonus over all the accounts and affairs of the kingdom. He was cupbearer, keeper of the signet, steward and overseer of accounts, placed next to the king, and he requested Tobit, who then came to Nineveh.

Tobit did many alms deeds for his kindred and nation, giving his bread to the hungry and his garments to the naked. He also gave a third tenth to those to whom it was appropriate, as his father's mother Deborah had commanded him after he was left an orphan.

l: burial of the dead (Tobit's burying), Tobit, Tobit / Chapter 1
s: Tobit buried any of his race found dead and thrown out on the wall of Nineveh, and privately buried those Sennacherib killed after they fled from Judea. When a Ninevite told the king, Tobit hid and withdrew in fear, and all his goods were forcibly taken.

The narrator, who has returned home with his wife Anna and son Tobias restored to him, sits down to a Pentecost feast and sends Tobias to find a poor kinsman who remembers the Lord. Tobias reports that a man of their race has been strangled and cast out in the marketplace, so the narrator takes the body into a chamber until sunset and then buries it, recalling Amos's prophecy about feasts turning to mourning. His neighbors mock him for burying the dead again despite the danger. After sleeping by his courtyard wall, sparrows drop warm dung into his open eyes and white films form, and physicians cannot help him, though Achiacharus supports him until he goes to Elymais. Anna weaves cloth for wages and brings home a kid as a gift, but the narrator suspects it is stolen and demands she return it, and she rebukes him by asking where his alms and righteous deeds are.

Tobias is the narrator's son, restored to him at the Pentecost feast. His father sends him to find a poor kinsman for dinner, and he returns to report that a man of their race has been strangled and cast out in the marketplace.

Anna, the narrator's wife, is restored to him and weaves cloth in the women's chambers, sending the work back to its owners. She is paid wages and given a kid, and when her husband doubts her and demands its return she rebukes him, asking where his alms and righteous deeds are and saying he and his works are known.

The narrator sits down to a Pentecost feast but leaves it to take in a strangled kinsman, then buries him at sunset after eating in heaviness and recalling Amos's prophecy. Mocked by neighbors, he sleeps polluted by his courtyard wall and loses his sight to sparrow dung. He later accuses Anna of bringing home a stolen kid and is ashamed of her, and she turns his own righteousness back on him.

l: poor man (kinsman of the narrator), Tobit, Chapter 2
s: The poor man is a member of the narrator's race who has been strangled and cast out in the marketplace. The narrator takes him up into a chamber until the sun sets and then buries him.

l: burial of the strangled man, Tobit, Chapter 2
s: After sunset the narrator digs a grave and buries the strangled kinsman, weeping. His neighbors mock him, saying he is no longer afraid of being put to death for this and yet buries the dead again.
Unknown to the narrator, sparrows nested in the wall of his courtyard where he slept. Their warm dung fell into his open eyes and caused white films to form.

White films come over the narrator's eyes after the sparrows' dung drops into them as he sleeps uncovered by the wall. Physicians cannot help him, but Achiacharus nourishes him until he goes into Elymais.

The kid is given to Anna along with her wages for weaving, and it cries when it reaches the house. The narrator suspects it is stolen and insists it be returned to the owners, while Anna says it was a gift beyond her wages.

In Chapter 3, Tobit, grieved and weeping, prays to the Lord, acknowledging His righteous judgments, asking Him not to take vengeance for his sins and those of his fathers, and requesting release from life through death. The same day in Ecbatana of Media, Sarah the daughter of Raguel is reproached by her father's maidservants because Asmodaeus the evil spirit has killed her seven husbands before they lay with her. Sarah considers hanging herself but refrains out of concern for her father's old age, and instead prays by the window, declaring her purity and asking to be released from the earth or shown pity. Both prayers are heard before the glory of God, and Raphael is sent to heal Tobit's eyes, give Sarah as wife to Tobias son of Tobit, and bind Asmodaeus.

Tobit is grieved and weeps, then prays to the Lord, confessing the righteousness of God's judgments and asking not to be punished for his own sins and those of his fathers. He asks to be released from life by death because of false reproaches and sorrow. His prayer is heard, and Raphael is sent to scale the white films from his eyes. At that time he returns and enters his house.

Sarah, daughter of Raguel in Ecbatana of Media, is reproached by her father's maidservants for having had seven husbands die. She grows so grieved that she thinks of hanging herself, but desists because it would bring sorrow on her father, her only parent mentioned. She prays by the window, claims purity, and asks to be released from the earth or shown pity. Her prayer is heard, and she is to be given as wife to Tobias; she comes down from her upper chamber.
Asmodaeus is the evil spirit who killed Sarah's seven husbands before they had lain with her. Raphael is sent to bind him, because Sarah belongs to Tobias by inheritance.
Raphael is sent to heal both Tobit and Sarah. His tasks are to scale the white films from Tobit's eyes, to give Sarah to Tobias as wife, and to bind the evil spirit Asmodaeus.
Tobias, son of Tobit, is named as the one to whom Sarah is to be given as wife. The text says it belonged to him to inherit her.

The Lord is addressed in both prayers as righteous, with works and ways of mercy and truth, and as judging true and righteous judgment forever. He hears the prayers of Tobit and Sarah before His glory and sends Raphael to heal them both.

l: seven men (Sarah's previous suitors), Tobit, Chapter 3
s: Sarah's seven husbands were each killed by Asmodaeus before they had lain with her. Their deaths cause the maidservants to accuse Sarah of strangling them and are the source of her reproach and despair.

Tobit's prayer praises the Lord's righteous judgments and asks that he not be punished for his sins and those of his fathers, who were given over to plunder, captivity, death, and reproach among the nations. He asks that his spirit be taken so he may be released from distress and go to the everlasting place. It is heard before the glory of God.

Sarah's prayer, made by the window, blesses the Lord's name and asks that she be released from the earth and hear no more reproach. She declares herself pure from sin with man and notes she is her father's only daughter with no heir. If death is not pleasing to God, she asks for regard and pity. It is heard before the glory of God.

Tobit, believing he may die, remembers the money he left in trust with Gabael in Rages of Media and calls his son Tobias to instruct him. He tells Tobias to bury him, honor his mother and bury her in the same grave, and to remember the Lord God and do righteousness all his days. He urges generous alms-giving according to one's means, marriage to a wife from the seed of his fathers rather than a strange wife, prompt payment of wages, avoiding drunkenness, and seeking wise counsel. Tobit then explains the ten talents of silver left with Gabael the son of Gabrias, and reassures Tobias that though they are poor, he has much wealth if he fears God and avoids sin.

Tobit remembers the money left with Gabael and, saying he has asked for death, decides to instruct his son Tobias before he dies. He gives Tobias commands about honoring his mother, righteousness, alms, marriage, wages, drunkenness, and counsel, and explains the ten talents of silver. He reassures Tobias that poverty is no cause for fear if he fears God.

Tobias is called by his father Tobit and receives a long set of instructions, including to bury Tobit, honor his mother, give alms, and marry within his father's kindred. He is told about the ten talents of silver with Gabael and assured he has much wealth if he fears God and avoids sin.
Gabael, called the son of Gabrias, is the man at Rages of Media with whom Tobit left money in trust. Tobit tells Tobias about this deposit of ten talents of silver.

The Lord God is the one Tobias is told to be mindful of all his days and to bless at all times, asking that his ways be made straight. He is described as the giver of all good things who humbles whom he will, and whose face will not turn from the one who does not turn from the poor.

l: ten talents of silver (Tobit's silver), Tobit, Chapter 4
s: The ten talents of silver were left in trust by Tobit with Gabael the son of Gabrias at Rages of Media. Tobit recalls it and explains it to Tobias before he dies, while telling him that true wealth lies in fearing God.

Tobit urges Tobias to give alms according to his abundance, or from even a little, without an envious eye and without turning from any poor man. He says it lays up a good treasure against necessity, delivers from death and darkness, and is a good gift in the sight of the Most High. He also tells him to give bread to the hungry and garments to the naked.

Tobit warns Tobias against fornication and tells him to take a wife from the seed of his fathers, not a strange wife outside his father's tribe. He cites Noah, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who took wives of their kindred and were blessed in their children, and tells Tobias not to scorn his kindred.

Tobit instructs Tobias to do righteousness all the days of his life and not follow the ways of unrighteousness. He says that those who do what is true will see their deeds prosper, and that doing what pleases God and departing from sin brings true wealth.

Tobias tells his father Tobit he will obey, but asks how he can collect the money since he does not know the man who holds it. Tobit gives him the handwriting and tells him to find a companion to travel with him, promising wages. Tobias finds Raphael, who is an angel though Tobias does not know it, and Raphael says he knows the way to Rages of Media. Tobit questions the man's tribe, accepts his claim to be Azarias, son of Ananias, agrees to pay a drachma a day plus necessities, and sends the two off with a blessing, the young man's dog going with them. Tobit's wife Anna weeps at losing their son, but Tobit reassures her that a good angel will accompany Tobias and bring him back safe, and she stops weeping.

Tobias promises to do all his father commands but asks how he can receive the money when he does not know the man. He finds a traveling companion, Raphael, without knowing he is an angel, prepares for the journey, and departs with him, his dog following.

Tobit gives Tobias the handwriting and tells him to find a man to go with him, offering wages. He questions the hired man's tribe and family, accepts him as kindred, agrees to pay a drachma a day plus necessities and more if both return safe, and blesses the journey. He comforts Anna by saying a good angel will go with their son and bring him back safely.

Raphael is identified as an angel whom Tobias does not recognize when he finds him. He agrees to go with Tobias, says he knows the way well and has lodged with Gabael, and tells Tobit he is Azarias, son of Ananias the great, of Tobit's kindred. Tobit agrees to pay him a drachma a day, and he departs with Tobias.

Anna weeps when Tobias is sent away, calling him the staff of their hand and saying money should be as refuse compared to their child. She says what the Lord has given them is enough, and she stops weeping after Tobit assures her that Tobias will return safe with a good angel.
Rages of Media is the destination where the money is to be collected. Tobias asks his companion whether he knows those places well, and Raphael answers that he knows the way well.

l: ten talents of silver (Tobit's silver), Tobit, Chapter 5
s: Tobias worries he cannot receive the money since he does not know the man who holds it. Tobit gives him the handwriting and instructs him to go and receive it, and Anna says they should not be greedy to add money to money.

l: journey to Rages (Tobias's journey), Tobit, Chapter 5
s: Tobias finds a companion for the journey, and Tobit hires him at a drachma a day with necessities and a promised addition if both return safe. Tobias prepares, and he and Raphael depart with the dog after Tobit's blessing that God and his angel will prosper the way. Tobit assures Anna that the journey will be prospered and Tobias will return safe and sound.

On their journey, the young man (later named Tobias) and the angel, who is called Brother Azarias, stop at the river Tigris, where a fish leaps out to swallow the young man. At the angel's command he seizes it, hauls it ashore, cuts it open and keeps the heart, liver and bile; they roast and eat the fish. The angel explains that burning the heart and liver drives away a demon or evil spirit, and that the bile heals white films in the eyes. Near Rages the angel says they will lodge with Raguel, a kinsman whose only daughter Sarah should be given to Tobias as wife. Tobias fears the demon that killed Sarah's seven earlier husbands, but the angel tells him to burn the heart and liver in the bride-chamber and to pray to God, and Tobias comes to love Sarah.

Tobias, called the young man, seizes the fish that leaps from the Tigris at the angel's command, cuts it open, and keeps its heart, liver and bile. He learns of Sarah and fears dying like her seven previous husbands, since he is his parents' only son, but the angel reassures him. After hearing the angel's instructions he loves Sarah and his soul is strongly joined to her.

Azarias, the young man's companion who is addressed as brother, commands him to grab the fish and to keep its heart, liver and bile. He explains their uses against demons and eye films, proposes that Sarah be given to Tobias, and says he will speak to Raguel. He tells Tobias how to drive off the demon in the bride-chamber and assures him that God will save them.

Raguel is named as a kinsman of Tobias with whom they will lodge near Rages, and as the father of an only daughter, Sarah. The angel says that under the law of Moses Raguel may not marry her to anyone else, or he would be liable to death, because the inheritance belongs to Tobias.

Sarah is Raguel's only daughter, described by the angel as fair and wise, and a kinswoman whose inheritance belongs to Tobias. Tobias has heard she was given to seven men who all perished in the bride-chamber. The angel says she will be given to Tobias as wife that night, that she was prepared for him from the beginning, and that he will save her.

A fish leaps out of the river Tigris and would have swallowed Tobias, but he grabs it at the angel's command and hauls it onto land. It is cut open for its heart, liver and bile, and the rest is roasted and eaten by Tobias and the angel.

l: incense ashes and fish heart and liver (Tobias's smoke), Tobit, Chapter 6
s: The heart and liver are kept by Tobias at the angel's order. The angel says that burning them as smoke before a man or woman troubled by a demon or evil spirit will make the affliction flee. He instructs Tobias to lay some on the ashes of incense in the bride-chamber so the smoke drives off the demon for good.

The demon loves Sarah and, as Tobias has heard, harms only those who come to her, so that her seven husbands died in the bride-chamber. The angel says it will smell the smoke of the fish's heart and liver, flee, and never come again.

l: marriage of Tobias and Sarah, Tobit, Chapter 6
s: The angel proposes that Sarah be given to Tobias as wife, arguing that she is his kinswoman and that the law of Moses requires it, and says it will take place that night, with the celebration after their return from Rages. Tobias fears the fate of Sarah's earlier husbands but is told to burn the fish's heart and liver and to pray with her to God. He comes to love her.

Tobias and his companion, whom Tobias calls Azarias, arrive at Ecbatana and are welcomed at the house of Raguel by Sarah. Raguel notices that Tobias resembles his cousin Tobit, and when the travelers say they are Naphtali's descendants from Nineveh and that Tobit is alive and well, Tobias reveals Tobit is his father. Raguel and his household weep on hearing Tobit is blind, then feast on a ram. Tobias asks that the matter discussed on the road be settled, and Raguel warns that seven relatives who married Sarah died in the night, but Tobias refuses to eat until a covenant is made. Raguel gives Sarah to Tobias as wife under the law of Moses and writes and seals a contract, and afterward Edna prepares another chamber and comforts the weeping Sarah.

Raguel receives Tobias and his companion at his house in Ecbatana, notices that Tobias resembles his cousin Tobit, and weeps on learning Tobit is blind. He discloses that seven relatives who married his daughter died in the night, yet agrees to give Sarah to Tobias under the law of Moses, blesses them, and writes and seals a contract.

Tobias arrives at Raguel's house, identifies himself as Tobit's son, and urges Raphael (called Azarias) to raise the matter discussed on the road. He refuses to eat until a covenant is made, then receives Sarah as his wife with Raguel's blessing.
Addressed by Tobias as Brother Azarias, he travels with Tobias to Ecbatana. At Tobias's urging he presents the matter discussed on the road to Raguel.

Sarah meets the travelers, greets them, and brings them into the house. Her father gives her by the hand as wife to Tobias, and she is then led to another chamber, weeping, where her mother comforts her.

Edna, Raguel's wife, hears her husband remark on Tobias's resemblance to Tobit, and weeps with the household at the news of Tobit's blindness. She prepares the other chamber, takes in her weeping daughter, and comforts her, praying that the Lord of heaven and earth give her favor.
Tobit is described by Raguel as his cousin and brother, and the travelers confirm he is alive and in good health. It is learned that he has lost his sight, which grieves Raguel and his household.

l: seven men (Sarah's previous suitors), Tobit, Chapter 7
s: Raguel reveals that he gave Sarah to seven men of their relatives. Each of them died in the night whenever he came in to her.

l: marriage contract (Tobias and Sarah's), Tobit, Chapter 7
s: After giving Sarah to Tobias, Raguel takes a book, writes a contract, and seals it. The eating begins after this.

After supper, Tobias is brought to his bride. Remembering Raphael's instructions, he burns the fish's heart and liver on incense ashes, and the smell makes the demon flee to the uppermost parts of Egypt, where the angel binds it. Tobias and his bride then pray together for God's mercy, and they sleep. Meanwhile Raguel digs a grave, fearing Tobias will die, but a maidservant finds them both alive, so Raguel blesses God and has the grave filled. He holds a fourteen-day wedding feast and swears that Tobias must stay until it ends, after which Tobias will receive half of Raguel's goods and go safely to his father.

Tobias is brought in to his bride after supper and, remembering Raphael's words, burns the fish's heart and liver on incense ashes to drive off the demon. He then rises and leads his bride in prayer, asking God for mercy and to grow old with her, and they sleep through the night. Raguel swears he must stay fourteen days and will then receive half of Raguel's goods and leave safely for his father.

Raguel digs a grave in the night, fearing that Tobias will die. After a maidservant reports that Tobias is alive, he blesses God for his mercy, orders the grave filled, and keeps a fourteen-day wedding feast. He swears Tobias must stay until the feast ends, then take half his goods to his father, with the rest to follow when Raguel and his wife die.

Sarah, called "Sister" by Tobias, is the bride he is brought in to after supper; she is not named in this chapter. She joins his prayer, saying "Amen," and sleeps with him through the night. The maidservant finds her alive and sleeping with him, and Raguel calls her and Tobias the only begotten children of their parents.
The demon smells the smoke from the burned fish heart and liver and flees into the uppermost parts of Egypt. The angel then binds it there.

God is addressed in Tobias's prayer as God of the fathers, with a holy and glorious name, who made Adam and gave him Eve as a helper. Raguel blesses God for gladness and for having dealt with them according to his great mercy, not as he suspected. Raguel also asks him to show mercy to the two only children and to fulfill their lives in health.

l: incense ashes and fish heart and liver (Tobias's smoke), Tobit, Chapter 8
s: Tobias, remembering Raphael's words, puts the heart and liver of the fish on the ashes of the incense and makes smoke with them. The smell drives the demon away into the uppermost parts of Egypt.
Raguel digs the grave at night, saying "Lest he also should die." Once the maidservant reports that Tobias is alive, Raguel commands his servants to fill it, so it goes unused.

l: wedding feast (Tobias and Sarah's wedding feast), Tobit, Chapter 8
s: Raguel keeps the wedding feast for fourteen days. Before it ends he swears that Tobias must not leave until all fourteen days are fulfilled, after which Tobias may take half of Raguel's goods and go in safety to his father.

l: Tobias and Sarah's marriage prayer, Tobit, Chapter 8
s: Tobias rises from the bed and asks his bride to rise and pray for the Lord's mercy on them. He blesses God, recalls that God made Adam and gave him Eve as a helper, and says he takes his sister not for lust but in truth, asking to find mercy and grow old with her. She says "Amen" with him, and they sleep.

Tobias calls Raphael, whom he addresses as Brother Azarias, and asks him to take a servant and two camels to Gabael in Rages of Media to collect money for him and bring Gabael to the wedding feast. Tobias explains that Raguel has sworn he must not leave, and that his father counts the days and will be very grieved if he is delayed. Raphael goes, lodges with Gabael, and hands over the handwriting, and Gabael brings out the sealed bags of money and gives them to him. Raphael and Gabael rise early the next morning and travel together to the wedding feast, where Tobias blesses his wife.

Tobias sends Raphael, whom he calls Brother Azarias, to Rages of Media to collect his money from Gabael and bring Gabael to the wedding feast. He says he cannot leave because Raguel has sworn he must not depart, and he worries that his father, who counts the days, will be grieved by a long delay. When Raphael and Gabael arrive at the feast, Tobias blesses his wife.

Raphael, addressed as Brother Azarias, is told by Tobias to take a servant and two camels to Gabael in Rages of Media. He lodges with Gabael, gives him the handwriting, and receives the sealed bags of money. He then rises early and returns with Gabael to the wedding feast.

Gabael is in Rages of Media and is to hand over Tobias's money. After Raphael lodges with him and gives him the handwriting, he brings out the sealed bags and gives them to Raphael. He then rises early and goes with Raphael to the wedding feast.

Rages of Media is the place where Gabael is, and Tobias directs Raphael to go there to receive the money. Raphael travels there, lodges with Gabael, and collects the bags before the return journey to the wedding feast.

l: ten talents of silver (Tobit's silver), Tobit, Chapter 9
s: The money is held by Gabael in bags with their seals, and Tobias sends Raphael to receive it for him. Raphael presents the handwriting, and Gabael brings out the sealed bags and gives them to him. The money is then carried back toward the wedding feast.

l: wedding feast (Tobias and Sarah's wedding feast), Tobit, Chapter 9
s: The wedding feast is the occasion Tobias wants Gabael to attend, and he stays because Raguel has sworn that he must not depart. Raphael and Gabael rise early and arrive at the feast together, and Tobias blesses his wife.

Tobit counts the days of his son Tobias's journey and worries when Tobias does not return, fearing he is detained or that Gabael has died. Tobit's wife is convinced the child has perished, goes out daily to the road, refuses to eat by day, and weeps through the nights. When the fourteen days of the wedding feast that Raguel had sworn are over, Tobias insists on leaving despite Raguel's offer to send word to his parents instead. Raguel gives Tobias his wife Sarah along with half his goods, servants, cattle and money, and blesses them. Raguel and Edna charge Sarah to honor her in-laws, and Edna asks Tobias not to cause Sarah grief.

Tobit counts the days of his son's journey and, when Tobias does not return, worries that he is detained or that Gabael has died and cannot give him the money. He is very grieved, but tells his wife to hold her peace and not worry, saying Tobias is in good health.

Tobias, after the fourteen days of the wedding feast that Raguel had sworn he would spend there, asks to be sent away because his parents look no more to see him. He refuses Raguel's offer to send word to his father instead and insists on going home. Raguel gives him Sarah and half his goods, and Edna asks him not to cause Sarah grief.

Raguel, who had sworn that Tobias should spend fourteen days of wedding feast there, first asks him to stay and offers to send word to Tobias's father, but yields when Tobias insists. He gives Tobias his wife Sarah and half his goods, servants, cattle and money, blesses them, and tells his daughter to honor her father-in-law and mother-in-law, then kisses her.

Sarah is given to Tobias by her father Raguel, together with half his goods, servants, cattle and money. Raguel tells her to honor her father-in-law and mother-in-law as her parents and kisses her, and her mother Edna commits her to Tobias in special trust, asking that he not cause her grief.

Tobias, blessing God for a prosperous journey, leaves Raguel and Edna and travels with Raphael toward Nineveh. Raphael tells Tobias to run ahead with the bile of the fish and explains how to use it on his father's eyes. Anna sees her son coming and runs to embrace him, and Tobias anoints Tobit's eyes with the bile so that the white films peel away and Tobit sees his son. Tobit blesses God and his holy angels, then goes out to the gate of Nineveh to welcome his daughter-in-law Sarah, and the wedding feast of Tobias is kept for seven days with joy among the kindred, including Achiacharus and Nasbas.

Tobias leaves Raguel and Edna blessing God and travels with Raphael to Nineveh, running ahead with the bile of the fish in hand. He anoints his father Tobit's eyes with it, saying "Cheer up, my father," and is seen by him, then tells his father the great things that happened in Media. His wedding feast is kept for seven days with great gladness.

Tobit goes toward the door and stumbles, but his son takes hold of him and rubs bile on his eyes. The white films peel away, he sees Tobias, weeps, and blesses God and his holy angels. He then goes out to meet Sarah at the gate of Nineveh, gives thanks publicly, and blesses her, and those who see him marvel that he has received his sight.

Raphael urges Tobias to run ahead of his wife and prepare the house, and to carry the bile of the fish. He announces that Tobit will open his eyes and instructs Tobias to anoint them, explaining that the pricking will make Tobit rub them and the white films fall away.

Anna sits watching the path for her son and sees him coming, telling Tobit that Tobias approaches with the man who went with him. She runs to Tobias, falls on his neck, and says she is ready to die now that she has seen him, and they both weep.
Sarah, Tobit's daughter-in-law, arrives near Nineveh and is met by Tobit at the gate. He welcomes her as daughter, blesses her and her father and mother, and blesses God who brought her to them.

God is blessed by Tobias for prospering his journey and by Tobit for scourging and then having mercy on him, as shown in the restoring of his sight. Tobit gives thanks before the people because God showed him mercy, and he also blesses God's holy angels.

l: bile of the fish, Tobit, Chapter 11
s: Tobias is told to carry the bile of the fish in his hand as they near Nineveh. Raphael explains that anointing Tobit's eyes with it will prick them, so that he rubs them and the white films fall away. Tobias rubs it on his father's eyes, and it is the means by which the films peel away.

l: healing (Raphael's cure of Tobit's household), Tobit, Chapter 11
s: Tobit's blindness is cured when his eyes begin to hurt after the bile is applied, he rubs them, and the white films peel away from the corners. He sees Tobias, calls it God's mercy after scourging, and the people of Nineveh marvel when they see him go out. The event brings joy to his kindred.

Tobit tells his son Tobias to pay the man who accompanied him his wages, and Tobias suggests giving him half of everything brought back, citing the safe journey, the cure of his wife and Tobit, and the recovered money. Tobit agrees and the angel is told to take half. The companion then privately urges both to bless and thank God, teaches that alms, prayer with fasting, and righteousness are good, and reveals that he is Raphael, one of the seven holy angels, who presented their prayers and was with Tobit when he buried the dead. Tobit and Tobias fall on their faces in fear, but Raphael reassures them, says he came by God's will, that he only appeared to eat and drink, and that he is ascending to the one who sent him, and tells them to write down all that has happened. He vanishes, and they confess the great works of God.

Tobit calls Tobias and insists that the man who went with him be paid his wages and more. He agrees that half of what was brought back is due, and has the angel told to take it. After Raphael's revelation, Tobit falls on his face in fear, is told to bless God and write down what happened, and afterward confesses God's wonderful works.

Tobias proposes giving the companion half of all that he brought back, recalling that the man led him safely, cured his wife, brought the money, and cured Tobit. He is told privately with Tobit to bless God, falls on his face in fear at Raphael's revelation, and afterward confesses with Tobit the works of God.

Raphael, who had accompanied them, is offered half of all that was brought. He reveals his identity as one of the seven holy angels who present the saints' prayers before God's glory, says he brought the memorial of Tobit's and Sarah's prayers and was with Tobit when he buried the dead, and says God sent him to heal Tobit and Sarah. He reassures them, says he only appeared to eat and drink, instructs them to write everything in a book, and ascends to God, after which they see him no more.

God is the one whose works are to be revealed gloriously and whom Tobit and Tobias are told to bless forever. He sent Raphael by his will to heal Tobit and Sarah, and the Holy One received the memorial of their prayers. Raphael ascends to him who sent him.

l: wages of the angel (Raphael's wages), Tobit, Chapter 12
s: Tobit says the companion must have his wages and more, and Tobias proposes half of what he brought back. Tobit agrees it is due and the angel is told to take half of all that was brought. The text records no response from Raphael to the offer, as he turns to teach and then reveals himself.

Raphael teaches that giving alms is better than laying up gold, and that it delivers from death and purges away all sin. Those who give alms and do righteousness will be filled with life, while sinners are enemies to their own life.

l: blessing and thanking God, Tobit, Chapter 12
s: Raphael urges Tobit and Tobias to bless, thank, and magnify God before all the living, and not to be slack in thanking him. He repeats the command to bless God forever and to give thanks as he ascends. Afterward the two confess God's great and wonderful works.

Tobit writes a prayer of rejoicing blessing God, the everlasting King, who both scourges and shows mercy. He calls the children of Israel to give thanks among the Gentiles, where they have been scattered, and promises that God will gather them again if they turn to him with their whole heart and soul. Tobit himself gives thanks in the land of his captivity and urges sinners to turn and do righteousness. He then addresses Jerusalem, the holy city, which will be scourged for the works of its sons but shown mercy again, and foretells that many nations will come with gifts. He closes by describing Jerusalem rebuilt with sapphires, emeralds, pure gold and paved streets of beryl, carbuncle and stones of Ophir, all crying 'Hallelujah!'

Tobit writes a prayer of rejoicing blessing God as the everlasting King. He gives thanks in the land of his captivity, shows God's strength and majesty to a nation of sinners, and urges them to turn and do righteousness. He also exalts God and calls on his own soul to bless the great King.

God is blessed as the one who lives forever, the everlasting King and King of heaven, and the Lord and Father of Israel forever. He scourges and shows mercy, leads down to the grave and brings up again, and no one escapes his hand. He will gather the scattered, turn to those who turn to him with their whole heart and soul, and exalt Jerusalem forever.

Jerusalem is addressed as the holy city that will be scourged for the works of its sons and then shown mercy again. Its tabernacle will be rebuilt with joy, those who love it will be blessed, and those who hate it are cursed. It will be built of precious stones and gold, and its streets will say 'Hallelujah!' and bless God who has exalted it forever.

The children of Israel are told to give thanks to God before the Gentiles, among whom he has scattered them. They are told to declare his greatness there because he is their Lord and Father forever. God will scourge them for their iniquities, show mercy again, and gather them out of all the nations.

Tobit foretells that Jerusalem will be built with sapphires, emeralds and precious stones, with walls, towers and battlements of pure gold. Its streets will be paved with beryl, carbuncle and stones of Ophir. Many nations will come from afar with gifts for the King of heaven, and generations will sing songs of rejoicing, while those who mourned its scourges will rejoice at seeing all its glory.

l: God's scourging and mercy, Tobit, Chapter 13
s: The prayer states that God scourges and shows mercy, leading down to the grave and bringing up again. He will scourge Israel for iniquities and Jerusalem for the works of its sons, and then will show mercy again, gathering the scattered and having mercy on the sons of the righteous. Turning to him with the whole heart and soul is said to bring him turning to them.

Tobit, after regaining his sight and growing very old, calls his son Tobias and his six grandsons and gives a final charge. He tells them to leave Nineveh for Media, because Jonah's prophecy of Nineveh's overthrow will come true, and he foretells the scattering of his kindred, the desolation and burning of Jerusalem and the house of God, and their later restoration with all nations turning to the Lord God. He urges them to keep the law, be merciful and righteous, and bury him and Anna decently, citing Aman and Achiacharus to show what alms and righteousness do. Tobit dies at 158, Tobias buries him and Anna, moves to Ecbatana in Media to Raguel, inherits the family possessions, and dies at 127 after hearing of the destruction of Nineveh by Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus.

Tobit, who lost his sight at fifty-eight and regained it after eight years, grows very old and gives alms and thanks to God. He charges Tobias and his grandsons to leave Nineveh, keep the law, and bury him and Anna, warning with the example of Aman and Achiacharus. He dies in bed at 158 and is buried magnificently by Tobias.

Tobias receives his father's final instructions to take his sons to Media and leave Nineveh. He buries Tobit magnificently, buries Anna with him, and departs with his wife and sons to Ecbatana to Raguel. There he grows old in honor, buries his parents-in-law, inherits their possessions and his father's, and dies at 127 after hearing of Nineveh's destruction.

Tobit says Nineveh will be overthrown, as the prophet Jonah spoke, and tells his family not to stay there. Before Tobias's death he hears that Nineveh has been destroyed and taken captive by Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus, and he rejoices over it.

Tobit directs Tobias to go into Media, where he believes there will be peace for a season rather than the overthrow coming on Nineveh. Tobias settles at Ecbatana of Media, where he grows old and dies.
Tobit foretells that Jerusalem will be desolate for a time. Afterward God will have mercy, bring the people back, and they will build up Jerusalem with honor.

Tobit foretells that the house of God in Jerusalem will be burned up and be desolate for a time. It will be rebuilt, though not like the former house until the times are fulfilled, and later will be built forever with a glorious building as the prophets spoke.

Tobit says the Lord God will again have mercy on his people and bring them back into the land. He foretells that all nations will turn to fear him truly, bury their idols, and bless him, and that his people will give him thanks. Tobit himself feared him more and more after regaining his sight.

l: Israelites (Tobit's kindred and people), Tobit, Chapter 14
s: Tobit foretells that his kindred will be scattered on the earth from the good land, but God will have mercy, bring them back, and rebuild Jerusalem. Those who love the Lord God in truth and righteousness will rejoice and show mercy to their kindred, and the Lord will exalt his people.

Tobit tells his children to consider what alms does and how righteousness delivers. He cites Manasses, who gave alms and escaped the snare of death set for him, while Aman fell into the snare and perished. Tobit himself gave alms after his sight was restored.

Tobit believes Jonah's words that Nineveh will be overthrown and uses this to urge his family to leave. Before Tobias dies he hears of the destruction, in which Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus took Nineveh captive, and he rejoices over it.

Chapter 1 of Greek Esther opens with Mordecai, a Jew serving in the palace at Susa, who sees a vision of two serpents, conflict among nations, and the exaltation of the lowly. He then uncovers a plot by the king's chamberlains Gabatha and Tharrha against King Ahasuerus, and the king has them executed and rewards Mordecai. Haman, favored by the king, seeks to harm Mordecai and his people. In the third year of his reign Ahasuerus holds a lavish feast of one hundred eighty days and a six-day banquet, while Queen Vashti holds a banquet for the women. On the seventh day Vashti refuses the king's summons, and on Memucan's advice the king issues a decree to remove her royalty and to ensure that wives honor their husbands.

Ahasuerus, great king over one hundred twenty-seven provinces, was saved from a plot by the chamberlains Gabatha and Tharrha after Mordecai informed him, and he had them executed and recorded the matter. In his third year he held a long feast and banquet displaying his wealth, then grew grieved and angry when Vashti refused his summons. He sought legal judgment from his advisers and followed Memucan's advice by issuing a decree sent to all provinces.

Vashti the queen made a banquet for the women in the palace while the king feasted. When the king, on the seventh day, sent chamberlains to bring her in to be crowned and shown to the princes and nations for her beauty, she refused to come. As a result the decree barred her from coming in to the king and gave her royalty to a better woman.

Mordecai, son of Jair, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Jew in Susa and one of the captives taken from Jerusalem, served in the king's palace and saw a vision of two serpents, battle among nations, and the exaltation of the lowly. He learned of the chamberlains' plot against the king and informed him, wrote an account of it, and was commanded to serve in the palace with gifts. He kept the vision in his heart, seeking to interpret it.

Haman, son of Hammedatha the Bougean, was honored in the king's sight and sought to harm Mordecai and his people because of the executed chamberlains. A Haman is also listed among the seven chamberlains whom the king sent on the seventh day to bring in Vashti.

Memucan told the king and princes that Vashti had wronged not only the king but all the rulers and princes, and that other wives would dishonor their husbands likewise. He advised a royal decree, unalterable under Median and Persian law, barring Vashti from the king and giving her royalty to a better woman. The king and princes were pleased and the king acted on this advice.

In his third year Ahasuerus made a feast for his friends, the nobles of the Persians and Medes, and the local governors, showing the wealth of his kingdom over one hundred eighty days. It was followed by a six-day banquet in the court of the king's house, richly adorned with fine linen, gold and silver couches, and costly cups. The banquet was not held according to appointed law but as the king desired.

On the seventh day of the banquet, Vashti refused to come with the chamberlains sent to bring her to the king, leaving him grieved and angry. The king asked his friends and the Persian and Median princes for a legal judgment, and they reported on what was proper to do about her failure to do what the king commanded.

On Memucan's advice, the king made a decree written according to the laws of the Medes and Persians, not to be altered, forbidding Vashti to come in to the king and giving her royalty to a better woman. It was sent through all the provinces in their own languages so that men might be feared in their own houses and wives would honor their husbands.

l: wives of the Persian and Median chiefs, Esther (Greek), Esther (Greek) / Chapter 1
s: Memucan warned that these women, having heard what Vashti said to the king, would dare to dishonor their husbands in the same way. The decree was meant to ensure that all women, poor to rich, would honor their husbands.

After the king's anger over Vashti subsides, his servants propose gathering beautiful young virgins from all the provinces to Susa so that the one who pleases him can replace her as queen. Mordecai, a Jew of the tribe of Benjamin who was carried captive from Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, has raised his cousin Esther, and she is brought to Hegai, keeper of the women, who favors her. At Mordecai's command Esther does not reveal her family or country, and she keeps her manner of life. After twelve months of purification she goes in to King Ahasuerus, who loves her above all the others, crowns her queen, and holds a seven-day banquet. When two chamberlains plot to kill the king, Mordecai discovers it and tells Esther, who informs the king; the chamberlains are hanged and Mordecai's goodwill is recorded in the royal library.

Esther, the foster daughter of Mordecai and daughter of Aminadab, was beautiful and was brought to Hegai, who favored her and gave her purification items and seven maidens. Following Mordecai's command she told no one her family or country and kept her manner of life. She went in to the king in the twelfth month, the seventh year of his reign, won his love beyond all the other virgins, and was crowned queen; she later reported Mordecai's discovery of the conspiracy to the king.

Mordecai is a Jew in Susa, son of Jairus, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the tribe of Benjamin, who was carried captive from Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. He raised Esther as his own, charged her not to reveal her family, walked daily by the women's court to learn her fate, and served in the courtyard. He discovered the chamberlains' plot and told Esther, and the king ordered his goodwill recorded in the royal library as a commendation.

King Ahasuerus's anger subsided and he no longer mentioned Vashti. He accepted his servants' plan to gather virgins, loved Esther above all, put the queen's crown on her, held a seven-day banquet for his friends and great men, and granted a remission of taxes. He examined and hanged the two chamberlains who sought to kill him and ordered Mordecai's goodwill noted in the royal library.

Two chamberlains of the king, chiefs of the body-guard, were grieved because Mordecai was promoted and sought to kill King Ahasuerus. The plot was discovered, and the king examined them and hanged them.

Two chamberlains, chiefs of the body-guard, plotted to kill the king out of grief over Mordecai's promotion. Mordecai discovered it and told Esther, who declared it to the king. The king examined and hanged the two men, and a note of Mordecai's goodwill was made in the royal library.

l: virgins (gathered for the king), Esther (Greek), Chapter 2
s: At the servants' suggestion, chaste, beautiful young virgins were to be selected by local governors in all the provinces and brought to Susa, into the women's apartment under the king's chamberlain, with purification and other needs supplied. Each served twelve months of purification, six with oil of myrrh and six with spices, before going in to the king in the evening and leaving in the morning for a second women's apartment, returning only if called by name. Esther found favor beyond all of them and became queen in place of Vashti.

King Ahasuerus promotes Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Bugaean, above all his friends, and everyone in the palace bows to him except Mordecai, who has told them he is a Jew. Enraged when palace officials report Mordecai's refusal, Haman plots to destroy all the Jews in Ahasuerus's realm and casts lots, which fall on the fourteenth day of Adar. Haman tells the king that a scattered nation with different laws disobeys the king and offers ten thousand talents of silver for its destruction. The king gives Haman his ring and tells him to keep the silver and treat the nation as he wills, so decrees in the king's name are sent by couriers to all 127 provinces ordering the Jews' destruction and plunder. The king and Haman drink while the city of Susa is confused.

King Ahasuerus highly honors Haman, sets his seat above all his friends, and orders that all bow to him. He accepts Haman's accusation against the Jews, gives Haman his ring to seal the decrees, tells him to keep the silver and treat the nation as he will, and then sits drinking with Haman while Susa is confused. The letter sent in his name presents the destruction as serving peace and order in the kingdom.

Haman is exalted by the king above all his friends, and he is enraged when Mordecai does not bow to him. He plots to destroy all the Jews, casts lots that fall on the fourteenth day of Adar, accuses the Jews before the king as a nation with differing laws, and offers ten thousand talents of silver. Receiving the king's ring, he commands the writing of the decrees sent to the provinces.

Mordecai refuses to bow down to Haman despite the king's order, and he ignores the palace officials who question him daily. He has shown them that he is a Jew, and they report his resistance to Haman. His refusal provokes Haman's rage and the plot against his people.

The Jews are described by Haman as a nation scattered among the nations whose laws differ and who disobey the king's laws. Haman plots to destroy them all under Ahasuerus's rule, and the king gives him authority to do as he will with them. They are targeted by decrees sent to 127 provinces for destruction and plunder on a set day in Adar.

l: Haman's decree of destruction, Esther (Greek), Chapter 3
s: Haman has the king's recorders write the decree on the thirteenth day of the first month, sealed with the king's ring and addressed to captains, governors and rulers from India to Ethiopia in their languages. It orders the Jews, with their wives and children, to be destroyed and their goods plundered, on the fourteenth day of Adar (the first day is also named in one verse). Copies are published in every province, and all nations are told to be ready for that day.

Mordecai learns of the decree against the Jews, tears his garments, puts on sackcloth and ashes, and cries out in the city, while mourning spreads through every province. Esther, troubled, sends clothes and then her chamberlain Hathach to learn the truth; Mordecai tells him of Haman's promise of ten thousand talents to the treasury and gives him a copy of the decree, urging Esther to plead with the king. Esther answers that approaching the king uncalled means death unless he extends his golden sceptre, but Mordecai warns that she and her father's house will perish if she stays silent and asks who knows whether she was made queen for this occasion. Esther agrees to go in contrary to the law and asks the Jews of Susa to fast three days, and Mordecai carries this out. The chapter closes with a long prayer by Mordecai and a long prayer by Esther, both appealing to the Lord God to save his people from destruction.

Mordecai tears his garments, puts on sackcloth and dust, cries out that a nation that has done no wrong is to be destroyed, and refuses the clothes Esther sends. He tells Hathach of Haman's promise of ten thousand talents, gives him a copy of the decree, and charges Esther to plead with the king, warning her that she and her father's house will perish if she keeps quiet. After Esther agrees, he organizes the fast and prays to the Lord, explaining that he refused to bow to Haman so as not to set the glory of man above the glory of God.

Esther is deeply troubled by the news, sends clothes to Mordecai, and dispatches Hathach to learn the truth. She first points out that entering uncalled means death, and she has not been called for thirty days, but after Mordecai's reply she resolves to go in to the king contrary to the law, even if she must die. She asks the Jews to fast for her, then humbles herself in mourning garments and ashes and prays that the Lord help her, asking for harmonious speech before the lion and professing that she hates the glory of transgressors and has not eaten at Haman's table.

Haman is described as holding the next place to the king and as having spoken against the Jews to cause their death. He promised the king ten thousand talents to be paid into the treasury so that he might destroy the Jews. Mordecai's prayer calls him arrogant, and Esther prays that the counsel of those against Israel be turned against themselves and that an example be made of the one who began to injure them. She also says she has not eaten at his table.

The king is the one before whom Esther must appear uncalled at risk of death unless he stretches out his golden sceptre, and he has not called her for thirty days. Haman promised him ten thousand talents for the destruction of the Jews. Esther prays that the Lord put harmonious speech into her mouth before the king, called the lion, and turn his heart to hate the one who fights against the Jews.

The Lord God is addressed in prayer by Mordecai as king over all, with all things in his power and no one able to resist him, and as the God of Abraham who redeemed Israel out of Egypt. Esther appeals to him as her only helper, recalls that he took Israel out of all nations as a perpetual inheritance, and says the people were delivered to enemies because they honored their gods. Both ask him to spare his people, turn mourning into gladness, and deliver them from death.

The Jews in every province where the decree was published respond with crying, lamentation, great mourning, sackcloth and ashes. Those in Susa are told by Esther to assemble and fast three days for her, and Mordecai carries this out. All Israel cries out with all their might, for death is before their eyes.

l: Haman's decree of destruction, Esther (Greek), Chapter 4
s: The decree has been published in Susa and in the provinces, and its publication causes mourning among the Jews everywhere. Mordecai sends a copy to Esther through Hathach as proof, along with word of Haman's promise of ten thousand talents to the treasury. Esther's and Mordecai's prayers describe it as an attempt by enemies to destroy God's inheritance and stop the mouth of those who praise him.

l: fast (Esther's and the Jews' three-day fast), Esther (Greek), Chapter 4
s: Esther tells Mordecai to assemble the Jews in Susa and have them fast for her, with no eating or drinking for three days, night and day, while she and her maidens also fast. She says that afterward she will go in to the king contrary to the law, even if she must die. Mordecai does all that she commanded, and prayers by him and Esther accompany the fast.

On the third day, Esther stops praying, dresses in her glorious apparel, and goes before the king, who looks at her with anger until God changes his spirit to gentleness. The king comforts her after she faints, extends the golden sceptre, and offers her up to half his kingdom. Esther asks that he and Haman come to a feast she will prepare, and at the banquet she postpones her request by inviting them again for the next day. Haman leaves glad but is enraged at seeing Mordecai the Jew in the court, and he boasts of his wealth and honor to his friends and his wife Zeresh. At their advice he has a fifty cubit gallows prepared so that Mordecai can be hanged on it.

Esther ceases praying on the third day, puts on her glorious apparel, and goes with two maids before the king, fearful in heart but beautiful in appearance. She faints before him, is comforted, and tells him she saw him as an angel of God. She invites the king and Haman to a feast, and at the banquet she defers her request by asking them to come again the next day.

Haman is invited with the king to Esther's feast and leaves glad and merry. Seeing Mordecai in the court enrages him, and he tells his friends and wife Zeresh of his wealth, his honor, and his exclusive invitation, saying these things do not please him while Mordecai remains. He is pleased by their advice to hang Mordecai and has the gallows prepared.
Mordecai the Jew is seen in the court by Haman, whose rage at the sight leads him to plot against him. Zeresh and Haman's friends advise that Mordecai be hanged on a gallows the next morning.

The king sits on his throne in glorious apparel, terrifying, and looks at Esther with intense anger. God changes his spirit to gentleness, so he springs from the throne, embraces and comforts her, and lays the golden sceptre on her neck. He offers her up to half his kingdom, and agrees to come with Haman to her feast and to return the next day.

l: gallows (Haman's gallows for Mordecai), Esther (Greek), Chapter 5
s: Zeresh and Haman's friends propose a gallows fifty cubits tall on which Mordecai would be hanged in the morning after Haman speaks to the king. The proposal pleases Haman, and the gallows is prepared.

Esther invites the king and Haman to a feast she prepares that day, and both attend. At the banquet the king asks her request twice, and she instead asks that they come again the next day to a further feast. Haman is glad to be the only one invited with the king.

The king cannot sleep and has the records read to him, discovering that Mordecai once exposed two chamberlains who plotted against Ahasuerus and that Mordecai was never rewarded. Haman arrives in the court intending to ask for Mordecai's hanging, but the king asks him what should be done for a man he wishes to honor. Assuming it is himself, Haman describes the king's robe and horse and a public proclamation, and the king orders him to do all this for Mordecai the Jew. Haman carries it out, then goes home mourning with his head covered, where his wife Zeresh and his friends warn that he will fall before Mordecai. The chamberlains then arrive to hurry Haman to Esther's banquet.

Mordecai's earlier report to the king about two chamberlains who sought to lay hands on Ahasuerus is found in the records, and the king learns he was never rewarded for it. He is dressed in the king's robe, mounted on the king's horse, and paraded through the city streets, then returns to the palace. Haman's wife and friends say that he is of the race of the Jews and that the living God is with him.

Haman comes to the court to ask the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows he prepared, but is asked what should be done for the man the king wishes to honor. Believing it is himself, he proposes the robe, horse and proclamation, and is then ordered to do all of it for Mordecai, which he does. He goes home mourning with his head covered, is told by Zeresh and his friends that he will assuredly fall, and is rushed by the chamberlains to Esther's banquet.

Ahasuerus, deprived of sleep by the Lord, has the records read to him and learns that Mordecai exposed the plot of the two chamberlains without being rewarded. He asks Haman what should be done for the man he wishes to honor, praises Haman's answer, and orders him to do it for Mordecai the Jew without neglecting a word of it.

l: robe of fine linen (the king's robe), Esther (Greek), Chapter 6
s: Haman proposes that the king's servants bring the robe of fine linen the king wears, to be given to a noble friend to dress the honored man. Haman takes the robe and dresses Mordecai in it.
Haman suggests the horse the king rides as part of the honor for the man the king loves. He takes the horse and mounts Mordecai on it to go through the city streets.

Haman devises the procession, thinking it is for himself: the honored man is dressed in the king's robe, mounted on the horse, and proclaimed through the city streets. The king orders it done for Mordecai, and Haman carries it out, proclaiming that this is what will be done for every man the king wishes to honor.

At a second banquet, Queen Esther asks the king to spare her life and her people, who she says have been sold for destruction and genocide. When the king demands to know who is responsible, Esther names Haman as the enemy, and Haman is terrified. The king leaves for the garden, and on returning finds Haman fallen on Esther's couch begging her for mercy, which the king takes as an assault. The chamberlain Bugathan tells the king about the fifty-cubit gallows Haman prepared for Mordecai, and the king orders Haman hanged on it. Haman is hanged there, and the king's wrath subsides.

At the second banquet, Esther asks the king to grant her life and her people's life, saying they have been sold for destruction, pillage, and genocide. She names Haman as the enemy, and Haman then begs her for mercy.

Haman is named by Esther as the wicked enemy and is terrified before the king and queen. He begs Esther for mercy and falls on her couch, which the king takes as an assault. He is then hanged on the gallows he had prepared for Mordecai.

The king offers Esther up to half his kingdom and asks who dared to threaten her and her people. He reacts angrily when he finds Haman on the couch by the queen, and after hearing about the gallows he orders Haman hanged on it. His wrath then subsides.

Mordecai is mentioned by the chamberlain Bugathan as the man who spoke concerning the king and for whom Haman prepared a fifty-cubit gallows. He does not act in this unit, and the gallows meant for him is used to hang Haman.

l: gallows (Haman's gallows for Mordecai), Esther (Greek), Chapter 7
s: Bugathan tells the king that a fifty-cubit gallows has been set up on Haman's property for Mordecai. The king orders Haman hanged on it, and Haman is hanged there.
